description: About Us: We are ambitious of beginner developers and space enthusiasts inspired by astrophysics and modern web technologies. We joined the NASA Space Apps Challenge to bridge the gap between complex astronomical datasets and the public by creating intuitive, interactive web tools.
summary:
SPHEREx Mover Search is a public web tool that shows how a patch of sky changes over time in NASA’s SPHEREx infrared data. Users enter coordinates or pick a quick target such as WISE 0855. The app retrieves SPHEREx images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, aligns them on one grid and plays them like a short video, so moving asteroids, comets and brown dwarfs stand out against fixed stars.
To help spot movers, it co-adds each of the six detector arrays separately, masks flagged pixels, subtracts a reference frame, flags moving candidates and overlays Gaia, AllWISE and known solar system objects. The field of view is adjustable, and every view is a shareable URL that can be embedded elsewhere. Data is queried live, so new releases appear without changing the tool.
This matters because SPHEREx images over a billion objects, far more than one person can examine. A simple, open tool lets students, volunteers and researchers join the search for moving objects.
details:
SPHEREx Mover Search lets anyone enter a sky position (RA and Dec), choose a ready-made target, or look up an object by name. The app queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx images of that patch of sky, places them on a common sky grid, sorts them by time, and plays them like a short video so that moving objects stand out against fixed stars. Users can choose the field of view and the number of cutouts, co-add each of the six detector arrays separately, weight frames by inverse variance, mask flagged pixels, subtract a reference frame (median or first frame), and set a detection threshold. Moving candidates are linked into tracks. Gaia stars, AllWISE sources, and known asteroids and comets (from SkyBoT) can be overlaid, and spectra are drawn with error bars. Every view has its own URL, so coordinates can be shared or embedded in other sites.

The tool works in a browser with nothing to install, requires no expertise in astronomical software, and turns a very large dataset into something a student or volunteer can read in seconds. Four extra tabs explain the mission, the instrument, small bodies, and infrared astronomy. The intended impact is to enable more people to take part in the search for asteroids, comets, and brown dwarfs in SPHEREx data, and to provide a base that others can build on.

It was developed with Python, Streamlit, Astropy, PyVO (TAP and SIA queries), NumPy, pandas, Altair, Matplotlib, and Pillow. The code was written in VS Code, stored on GitHub, and hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. Data sources include SPHEREx and IRSA, Gaia (ESA), and AllWISE.

The creative approach treats the 102 bands as extra signal (through per-detector co-adding) and combines blinking, subtraction, and automatic candidate tracks in one view, with a calm dark design and short explainers built into the page. Factors considered during development include data transfer time versus field of view, reliability (the app tries TAP first and then SIA, can retry unavailable services, and has a demo mode with artificial frames), ease of updates because data is queried live, and scientific caveats such as brightness changing between bands and flagged pixels. This is an unofficial educational project, not affiliated with NASA or Caltech.
